newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary can't meet low EU inflation - NBH president.
newsitem.headline: Hungary can't meet low EU inflation - NBH president.

text.p: Hungary and some other east European countries that are candidates for EU enlargement cannot be expected to have low single-digit inflation by next century, Hungary's central bank president said on Wednesday.

"If you really bear in mind that these countries have to meet the challenge of the 21st century, I believe it is not realistic to reach the low single-digit inflation, let's say of one to three percent, by the beginning of next century," NBH President Gyorgy Suranyi told a conference on EU enlargement.
Suranyi said Hungary's inflation, which the government hopes to bring below 10 percent year-on-year in 1998 from 18.9 percent in January, could be forced down "artificially".

"But I have serious doubts whether those countries which are able to reach very low inflationary targets in the foreseeable future...whether those targets can be taken as sustainable from the point of view of the external balances and internal financial and macroeconomic balances," Suranyi said.
Suranyi, speaking at a conference sponsored by ABN-AMRO Bank, also said Hungary and other East European front-runners for EU enlargement would not be a financial millstone for existing EU members.
He said it was "irrelevant" to compare costs of East European states joining the EU and the billions of dollars that Germany has spent absorbing former East Germany.

"Hungary and none of the other Central and East European countries have got demands for meeting the living standards of the European Union average in two or three years or even five years," Suranyi said.
"There is a need for a more gradual increase of the living standards over the real wage levels. Simply to bear this in mind it means the cost of enlargement has to be much lower."
He also said it would be a mistake to extend the EU's costly common agricultural policy to the new eastern European members.

"Personally I believe the European Union's agricultural policy is not sustainable in the medium and long term and it would be a really serious mistake to extend it towards the Central and East European countries," Suranyi said.

ABN-AMRO senior executive vice president Jaap Kamp said the bank is in favour of EU enlargement but does not think the EU would be willing to spend the large sums of money it spent on southern enlargement.
"We do not think a similar generosity can be expected," Kamp said. "The present EU members simply cannot afford it. And we doubt these funds are necessary to achieve the enlargement aims."
